comments.author: @Dina_tankar_mina_ord
comments.text:
Back when I was 16, around '93, I used to think that people who were into computers were nerds, and back then, "nerd" was definitely an insult. I only played video games on consoles, because for some reason that was considered okay and not lame, weird times. Anyway, there was this guy who brought me into the computer lab at high school to show me something cool. It was a game where you could run around in rooms from a first-person view. I was stunned, I’d never seen anything like it. And on top of that, you could play four people at the same time, in the same game, in the same room, yelling at each other. I was completely mind-blown. Of course, the game was Doom.

After that, I got more and more into computers and gradually ditched consoles, I haven’t looked back since. Then, when we got OpenGL graphics working on my PC for the first time, our jaws dropped. The pixels were smeared smooth, and everything ran at almost 40 FPS. Doom, Wolfenstein, Duke Nukem, and later Unreal were mind-blowing for their time. Tim Sweeney and John Carmack are, to game development, what Elon Musk has been to electric vehicles.

Being part of that era and watching computers evolve, from chunky, centimeter-sized pixels on a monochrome CRT monitor to Nanite, Lumen, and now AI-generated content, has been like living through a sci-fi journey across time. And honestly, as long as I don’t kick the bucket in the next five years, I think the coolest stuff is still just around the corner. Awesome times and what a ride.

I started making a game with AI a few days ago and I am blown away by the capabilities, I can see how the future is going to be incredible in coming years.

 I gave Claude a single prompt to create a Rouge-lite Horde survivor game using  basic graphics, then updated it in Copilot, before finally giving the code and all my ideas to Google Gemini, and Google Gemini took it farther than any other AI, Google Gemini is killing it right now. 

Now the game features a infinitely scrolling white background with Randomly spawning Black impassable Obstacle Chunks, A Player Character Cursor Triangle, and 6 enemy shape types, Square, Circle, Triangle, Diamond, Pentagon, and Hexagon, each with unique traits. Each run is 15 minutes long, featuring 3 mini Bosses and a final boss spawn. We even added Containers with Gold and various possible Power ups that can be collected, added a companion shape system to unlock new shapes to follow and assist the player, and 3 unique abilities the player can obtain after defeating each mini boss.

Like seriously, this extremely simple looking game that looks like it could have been on Atari, is so fun it's so addicting, and I can't wait to keep adding more to it.

comments.author: @torarinvik4920
comments.text: The AI game path although promising was someone abandoned by mainstream AI companies. They started out with that stuff in the 2010s but somewhat abandoned it when LLMs came because LLMs solved the problem of understanding language. That was the issue that they struggled to solve, and arguably the most important one. Personally I think the path of creating a cognitive architecture that can learn like humans starting very dumb, but having the ability to generalize few shot is the obvious way forward. The ability to learn from input, remember it, and apply it to novel situations, and adapt. It really shouldn't be focus on collecting as much data as possible and having monster training runs. If a model can continuously learn and compound knowledge and skills, then there really is no data wall as the real world is extremely rich in data, internet too. They really should focus on making models be able learn more from less data, rather than training on more data.
